blocks.text: A tourniquet is a device used to temporarily restrict venous or arterial blood flow, depending on its type and application.
In routine medical OSCEs, the tourniquet most commonly refers to the elastic strap used during venepuncture to make superficial veins more prominent and easier to access.
OSCE objective: Identify the tourniquet, explain its types and uses, demonstrate safe application, recognize when it should be avoided, and describe complications and precautions in children.

items.text: Name: Tourniquet.
Classification: Device for temporary vascular compression.
Most common clinical type: Elastic venepuncture tourniquet.
Main purpose: To distend superficial veins temporarily, facilitating venepuncture and peripheral IV cannulation.

blocks.text: 1. Venepuncture tourniquet
An elastic strap applied proximal to a venepuncture site. It restricts venous return while generally permitting arterial inflow when used correctly.
2. Pneumatic surgical tourniquet
An inflatable cuff connected to a pressure-control device, used in selected operations on limbs to reduce blood flow to the operative field. It requires trained personnel and appropriate monitoring.
3. Emergency haemorrhage-control tourniquet
A purpose-designed device used to control life-threatening bleeding from a limb when indicated. It is fundamentally different from the simple elastic venepuncture strap.
Exam distinction: Never use an ordinary venepuncture tourniquet as a substitute for a proper emergency haemorrhage-control tourniquet.

items.text: Making superficial veins more visible and palpable before blood collection.
Facilitating peripheral IV cannulation.
Assisting venous access during selected blood sampling procedures.
Helping identify suitable veins in the antecubital fossa or forearm.
Surgical tourniquet: Reduces blood flow to an operative limb during selected procedures.
Emergency tourniquet: Controls life-threatening extremity haemorrhage when indicated.

blocks.text: For a routine medicine or pediatrics OSCE, concentrate primarily on the venepuncture tourniquet.
A basic elastic venepuncture tourniquet may have the following components:
1. Elastic strap
Produces adjustable compression around the limb.
2. Buckle or fastening mechanism
Secures the strap and allows rapid release. Designs differ between reusable and disposable models.
3. Release tab or mechanism, if present
Allows the tourniquet to be loosened quickly after venous access is obtained.
Some tourniquets are simple elastic strips without buckles. The essential features are sufficient strength, controlled compression and safe release.

items.text: Inexpensive and easy to use.
Rapidly improves the visibility and palpability of superficial veins.
Helps facilitate venepuncture and cannulation.
Portable and requires no electricity.
Available in disposable and reusable forms.
Quick-release designs allow rapid removal.
Excessive pressure can cause pain, bruising or tissue injury.
Prolonged application can alter some blood-test results through venous stasis.
Fragile veins may rupture or become difficult to access.
It may be difficult to identify veins in patients with dehydration, obesity, shock or poor peripheral perfusion.
Reusable tourniquets may transmit microorganisms if not cleaned appropriately.
It does not guarantee successful venepuncture.

blocks.text: Important laboratory point: Prolonged tourniquet application and repeated fist clenching can alter certain analytes, including potassium and some proteins. Follow the laboratory's collection protocol and avoid unnecessary delay.

items.text: Perform hand hygiene.
Confirm the patient's identity and explain the procedure.
Select an appropriate vein and inspect the limb.
Check for relevant restrictions, such as an existing arteriovenous fistula, a limb with a specific vascular-access precaution, or local tissue injury.
Choose a suitable tourniquet that is intact and clean.
Apply it proximal to the intended venepuncture site, generally around 7–10 cm above the site when anatomy permits.
Tighten it enough to impede venous return without unnecessarily restricting arterial inflow.
Confirm that the vein becomes more prominent and that the patient remains comfortable.
Release it promptly when it is no longer needed, following the appropriate sequence for the procedure.
Dispose of a single-use tourniquet or clean a reusable one according to infection-prevention policy.

blocks.text: Examiner's tip: A tourniquet should not be left tightly applied while you search repeatedly for a vein or prepare equipment unnecessarily.

subsections.subsection_title: 7. How to use a venepuncture tourniquet — step-by-step OSCE demonstration

blocks.text: Step 1 — Explain and prepare
Introduce yourself, confirm the patient using the required identifiers, explain the procedure and perform hand hygiene.
Step 2 — Select the site
Inspect and palpate the veins, commonly in the antecubital fossa or forearm. Avoid unsuitable areas or limbs with relevant vascular-access restrictions.
Step 3 — Apply the tourniquet
Place it approximately 7–10 cm proximal to the intended site when appropriate. Secure it so venous return is restricted without excessive compression.
Step 4 — Reassess the vein
Check that the vein is more prominent and palpable. Ask about discomfort and make sure the tourniquet is not excessively tight.
Step 5 — Proceed with venepuncture
Clean the skin and allow it to dry. Perform venepuncture using the appropriate equipment and local protocol. Release the tourniquet as soon as appropriate, generally before withdrawing the needle.
Step 6 — Complete safely
Withdraw the needle, apply pressure, dispose of the sharp immediately and check the site for bleeding or haematoma. Label and handle the specimen correctly.

content_groups.group_title: What to say during the demonstration

blocks.text: “I would apply the tourniquet proximal to the selected vein, using enough pressure to restrict venous return while preserving arterial inflow. I would confirm that the vein becomes prominent, avoid prolonged application, and release the tourniquet promptly when it is no longer required.”

content_groups.group_title: How long should it remain applied?

blocks.text: For routine venepuncture, aim to keep application to less than one minute where possible. If access is delayed, release it and reassess before trying again, following local policy.
The exact timing of release should follow the procedure and institutional protocol. For example, blood collection procedures have specific sequencing requirements.
Avoid applying a tourniquet to a limb when the procedure is contraindicated by local vascular-access policy. Examples include:

items.text: A limb with an arteriovenous fistula or graft used for haemodialysis.
A limb with a relevant vascular injury or severe circulatory compromise.
A site with significant local trauma, infection or skin damage.
A limb with specific restrictions following surgery or vascular procedures.

blocks.text: A history of mastectomy or lymph-node surgery requires individualized assessment and adherence to local policy; it should not automatically be treated as an absolute prohibition in every circumstance.

rows: Blood leaking into surrounding tissues, often associated with venepuncture trauma
Venous stasis can change selected analyte concentrations
Rare with routine use but possible with excessive compression
May occur if the tourniquet is excessively tight

content_groups.group_title: If the limb becomes painful, numb or discoloured

blocks.text: Release the tourniquet immediately, assess distal circulation and sensation, and escalate if symptoms persist or a vascular complication is suspected.
Do not confuse routine venepuncture practice with surgical tourniquet use. Surgical tourniquets require specific pressure settings, duration limits, trained supervision and monitoring.
Normal / satisfactory

items.text: Superficial vein becomes more visible and palpable.
Patient experiences minimal discomfort.
Distal circulation remains satisfactory.
Skin remains intact without unusual swelling or discoloration.
Tourniquet releases promptly.

blocks.text: Abnormal / concerning

items.text: Persistent pain, numbness or tingling.
Marked discoloration or swelling.
Distal circulation appears compromised.
Excessive bruising or petechiae.
The vein remains difficult to identify despite appropriate application.

blocks.text: Children, especially neonates and infants, require careful application because of their smaller limbs, delicate skin and limited vascular access.

items.text: Use an appropriately sized tourniquet: Avoid adult straps that produce excessive compression on a small limb.
Gentle pressure: Apply only enough compression to improve vein visibility.
Limit duration: Release promptly to minimize discomfort and venous stasis.
Skin protection: Avoid pinching, twisting or trapping the skin beneath the strap.
Distal circulation: Observe skin colour, temperature and perfusion.
Neonatal venepuncture: Some procedures may use alternative vein-visualization methods or specialized techniques; follow neonatal unit policy.
Distress reduction: Use caregiver support, distraction, positioning and other age-appropriate comfort measures.
Poor perfusion: In shock or severe circulatory compromise, superficial veins may be difficult to identify, and alternative vascular-access strategies may be required.

blocks.text: High-yield point: A tourniquet helps identify veins but does not correct hypovolaemia or poor circulation.

blocks.title: Use VEIN to remember safe tourniquet application:

items.text: V — Verify the patient and vascular-access precautions.
E — Ensure correct placement proximal to the site.
I — Inspect the vein and distal circulation.
N — Never leave it on longer than necessary.
Venepuncture tourniquet: Promotes venous distension.
Surgical tourniquet: Restricts limb blood flow under controlled conditions.
Haemorrhage-control tourniquet: Controls life-threatening limb bleeding.

blocks.text: These devices are not interchangeable.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Common OSCE questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is a tourniquet?
A device used to temporarily restrict blood flow. In routine venepuncture, an elastic tourniquet restricts venous return to make superficial veins more prominent.
Q2. Why is it applied above the venepuncture site?
To impede venous return from the distal limb and promote venous distension at the selected site.
Q3. Does a venepuncture tourniquet stop arterial flow?
It should not when correctly applied. Excessive tightness can compromise arterial inflow and cause harm.
Q4. How long should a routine venepuncture tourniquet remain on?
Aim for less than one minute where possible, releasing it promptly if access is delayed and following the relevant collection protocol.
Q5. Why can prolonged application affect laboratory results?
Venous stasis can alter the local concentration of some blood constituents and therefore affect certain measurements.
Q6. Name three complications.
Pain, bruising or petechiae, and altered laboratory results. Excessive compression can also compromise circulation.
Q7. Would you apply it over an AV fistula?
No. I would avoid applying a routine tourniquet to a haemodialysis access limb and follow the patient's vascular-access precautions.
Q8. What would you do if the patient reported numbness?
Release the tourniquet immediately, assess circulation and sensation, and escalate if symptoms persist.
Q9. How does a surgical tourniquet differ from a venepuncture tourniquet?
A surgical tourniquet uses a controlled pneumatic cuff to reduce limb blood flow during selected procedures. A routine venepuncture tourniquet is intended primarily to impede venous return.
Q10. Why must reusable tourniquets be cleaned?
They can become contaminated with blood or microorganisms and may transmit infection between patients if infection-prevention procedures are not followed.

items.text: Applying the tourniquet too tightly.
Placing it too close to the intended puncture site.
Leaving it on for too long.
Failing to inspect the limb for vascular-access restrictions.
Ignoring pain, numbness or skin discoloration.
Failing to release it promptly after obtaining access.
Reusing a contaminated tourniquet without appropriate cleaning.
Confusing a venepuncture tourniquet with an emergency haemorrhage-control device.

blocks.text: Examiner tip: State explicitly that the goal is to impede venous return while maintaining arterial inflow. This demonstrates understanding of the physiological principle rather than simple memorization.
